subject: Social Science (Exploring Society: India and Beyond, Part 2)

model_paper.paper_title: Chapter 1 Model Assessment - The Story of Indian Farming

section_a.title: Section A: Objective MCQs & Assertion-Reason (6 Marks)
section_a.instructions: Answer all questions. Each question carries 1 mark.

questions.question_text: Which cropping season in India relies on the South-West monsoon and is sown around June-July?
Black soil (Regur) is derived from which type of geological rock formation?
Which micro-irrigation method delivers water directly drop-by-drop to plant roots, significantly preventing evaporation losses?
What percentage of working women in rural India are engaged in agricultural operations?

Assertion (A): Over-extraction of groundwater through tube wells causes soil salinisation and falling water tables in arid regions.
Reason (R): Excessive tube-well irrigation brings deep minerals to the topsoil while evaporating rapidly under heat.
options: A) Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
B) Both A and R are true, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
C) A is true but R is false.
D) A is false but R is true.
questions.correct_option: A) Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
questions.marking_scheme: 1 Mark for identifying that both statements are factually correct and logically linked.

questions.question_text:
Assertion (A): Laterite soil is highly suitable for growing tea, coffee, and cashew nuts.
Reason (R): Laterite soil is formed by intense leaching caused by heavy rainfall in tropical regions.
options: A) Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
B) Both A and R are true, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
C) A is true but R is false.
D) A is false but R is true.
questions.correct_option: A) Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
questions.marking_scheme: 1 Mark for establishing that leaching leaves acidic, iron-rich residue suitable for plantation crops.

section_b.title: Section B: Short Answer Questions (10 Marks)
section_b.instructions: Answer all 5 questions. Each question carries 2 marks.

questions.question_text: Differentiate between Kharif and Rabi cropping seasons with respect to sowing time and two key crops.
questions.solution_and_marking_scheme:
Kharif: Sown in June-July (Monsoon onset); Key crops: Paddy (Rice), Cotton (1 Mark).
Rabi: Sown in Oct-Nov (Winter onset); Key crops: Wheat, Mustard (1 Mark).

questions.question_text: State the ancient agricultural wisdom expressed in the Sanskrit text Krishi Parashara.
questions.solution_and_marking_scheme: Krishi Parashara states that a farmer who cares diligently for livestock, visits fields daily, understands seasonal variations, selects good seeds, and works industriously is blessed with abundant yields (2 Marks).

questions.question_text: Explain why Alluvial soil is considered highly productive for agriculture in India.
questions.solution_and_marking_scheme:
1. Alluvial soil is deposited by major river systems, rich in potash, phosphoric acid, and humus (1 Mark).
2. It possesses a balanced loam texture offering optimal water retention and root aeration for crops like rice and sugarcane (1 Mark).

questions.question_text: Describe the Zaid cropping season and list two products harvested during this period.
questions.solution_and_marking_scheme: Zaid is a short summer cropping season between Rabi harvesting and Kharif sowing (March to June) (1 Mark). Products include watermelon, cucumber, muskmelon, and seasonal green vegetables (1 Mark).

questions.question_text: How does crop rotation help maintain long-term soil fertility without excessive chemical fertilizers?
questions.solution_and_marking_scheme: Rotating cereal crops with leguminous plants (like gram or pulses) fixes atmospheric nitrogen into the soil through root nodules, replenishing nutrient levels naturally and breaking pest cycles (2 Marks).

section_c.title: Section C: Long Answer & Analytical Questions (8 Marks)
section_c.instructions: Answer both questions. Each question carries 4 marks.

questions.question_text: Analyze the major soil types of India (Alluvial, Black, Red/Yellow, Laterite) in terms of their geographical distribution, characteristics, and crop suitability.
questions.solution_and_marking_scheme:
1. Alluvial Soil: Found in Indo-Gangetic plains & coastal deltas; rich in potash/humus; suitable for rice, wheat, sugarcane (1 Mark).
2. Black Soil (Regur): Volcanic origin in Deccan Trap (MH, GJ, MP); clayey texture with high moisture retention; ideal for cotton, jowar (1 Mark).
3. Red & Yellow Soil: Formed on crystalline igneous rocks in eastern/southern Deccan; red color due to iron diffusion; suitable for millets, pulses (1 Mark).
4. Laterite Soil: Formed by intense leaching in heavy rain zones (Western Ghats, Meghalaya); acidic nature; ideal for tea, coffee, cashew (1 Mark).

questions.question_text: Discuss the environmental hazards associated with over-irrigation and groundwater depletion, and propose three modern sustainable water management techniques.
questions.solution_and_marking_scheme:
Environmental Hazards (2 Marks):
- Excessive tube-well pumping causes drastic falling of underground water tables.
- Over-irrigation causes soil salinisation and waterlogging, destroying soil aeration.
Sustainable Solutions (2 Marks):
1. Adoption of drip and sprinkler micro-irrigation systems to reduce water waste by up to 60%.
2. Implementation of farm pond rainwater harvesting to recharge local aquifers.
3. Shifting to drought-tolerant crop varieties and practicing organic mulching.

section_d.title: Section D: Competency / Source-Based Case Study (6 Marks)
section_d.instructions: Read the passage carefully and answer the sub-questions that follow.
section_d.case_scenario: Passage: In a dry village in western Maharashtra, farmers traditionally relied on flood irrigation from open wells. Over time, water levels dropped by 50 feet, and the soil developed a white salty crust, reducing sugar cane yields. A local agricultural cooperative introduced a community watershed project. They installed rainwater harvesting tanks, switched 100 hectares of sugarcane to solar-powered drip irrigation, and introduced crop rotation with chickpea and soybean. Within three years, groundwater levels recovered by 12 feet, soil health improved, and farmers saved 40% on electricity and fertilizer costs.

sub_questions.question_text: What caused the white salty crust on the soil under traditional flood irrigation? (2 Marks)
sub_questions.solution_and_marking_scheme: Over-irrigation combined with rapid evaporation under solar heat brought dissolved ground salts to the topsoil layer, forming a saline crust that impaired root absorption (2 Marks).

sub_questions.question_text: Explain two ways drip irrigation solved the water scarcity problem in this village. (2 Marks)
sub_questions.solution_and_marking_scheme:
1. Drip irrigation applies water directly to plant root zones, preventing evaporation and weed growth water loss (1 Mark).
2. It delivers exact water quantities, cutting total consumption by over 40% and preventing groundwater over-extraction (1 Mark).

sub_questions.question_text: How did introducing chickpea and soybean in crop rotation improve soil fertility and lower costs? (2 Marks)
sub_questions.solution_and_marking_scheme: Chickpea and soybean are leguminous crops whose root nodules contain Rhizobium bacteria that fix atmospheric nitrogen into the soil. This naturally restores soil fertility and reduces the need for expensive chemical nitrogen fertilizers (2 Marks).

model_paper.paper_title: Chapter 2 Model Assessment - India and Her Neighbours

section_a.title: Section A: Objective MCQs & Assertion-Reason (6 Marks)
section_a.instructions: Answer all questions. Each question carries 1 mark.

questions.question_text: Which neighboring country shares the longest terrestrial land border (~4,096 km) with India?
What water channel separates peninsular India from Sri Lanka?

options: A) Security and Growth for All in the Region
B) South Asian Growth and Regional Aid
C) Strategic Alliance for Gulf and Asian Rivers

questions.question_text: Under the 1950 Treaty of Peace and Friendship, citizens of which country enjoy passport-free movement and work rights in India?

questions.marking_scheme: 1 Mark for establishing spiritual transmission via royal missions.

questions.question_text:
Assertion (A): India acts as a 'First Responder' during humanitarian disasters in South Asian and Indian Ocean nations.
Reason (R): India possesses geographic proximity, naval airlift capability, and a policy commitment to regional HADR support.
options: A) Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
B) Both A and R are true, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
C) A is true but R is false.
D) A is false but R is true.
questions.correct_option: A) Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.

section_b.title: Section B: Short Answer Questions (10 Marks)
section_b.instructions: Answer all 5 questions. Each question carries 2 marks.

questions.question_text: Name the seven nations that share land frontiers with India.
questions.solution_and_marking_scheme: Pakistan, Afghanistan, China, Nepal, Bhutan, Bangladesh, and Myanmar (2 Marks for all 7 named accurately).

questions.question_text: Define a 'maritime neighbour' and list two maritime neighbours of India.
questions.solution_and_marking_scheme: A maritime neighbour is a nation separated by an oceanic arm or channel rather than sharing a continuous land mass (1 Mark). Examples: Sri Lanka and Maldives (1 Mark).

questions.question_text: Explain two key features of the 1950 Indo-Nepal Treaty of Peace and Friendship.
questions.solution_and_marking_scheme:
1. Establishes an open border allowing citizens to travel without passports or visas (1 Mark).
2. Grants equal rights to reside, work, hold property, and trade in either nation (1 Mark).

questions.question_text: What is the primary objective of India's SAGAR policy in the Indian Ocean region?
questions.solution_and_marking_scheme: SAGAR aims to foster maritime security, maritime capacity building, joint anti-piracy surveillance, and sustainable Blue Economy growth among all Indian Ocean littoral states (2 Marks).

questions.question_text: How do hydroelectric energy projects foster economic cooperation between India and Bhutan?
questions.solution_and_marking_scheme: India assists Bhutan in developing clean hydroelectric dams (e.g., Chukha, Tala). Bhutan exports surplus clean electricity to India, generating major revenue for Bhutan while meeting India's power demands (2 Marks).

section_c.title: Section C: Long Answer & Analytical Questions (8 Marks)
section_c.instructions: Answer both questions. Each question carries 4 marks.

questions.question_text: Examine the civilisational, cultural, and spiritual links that connect India with South and Southeast Asian neighbours.
questions.solution_and_marking_scheme:
1. Spiritual Corridors: Spread of Buddhism from Bodh Gaya and Nalanda across Sri Lanka, Myanmar, Bhutan, Tibet, and Thailand (1 Mark).
2. Epics & Literature: Adaptations of Ramayana and Mahabharata in Southeast Asian theater and temple art (e.g., Wayang in Indonesia, Reamker in Cambodia) (1 Mark).
3. Linguistic & Scriptural Roots: Influence of Sanskrit, Pali, and Brahmi script on South Asian and Southeast Asian languages (1 Mark).
4. Architectural Styles: Shared temple construction techniques seen in Prambanan, Angkor Wat, and Sri Lankan stupas (1 Mark).

questions.question_text: Discuss India's role as a 'First Responder' during regional natural disasters, citing specific operational examples.
questions.solution_and_marking_scheme:
First Responder Framework (2 Marks):
- India provides immediate Humanitarian Assistance and Disaster Relief (HADR) within hours of crises in South Asia and Indian Ocean littoral states.
- Rapid deployment of naval ships, air force transport aircraft, field hospitals, mobile water purification units, and rescue engineering teams.
Specific Examples (2 Marks):
1. Operation Maitri (2015 Nepal Earthquake): Massive rescue, medical, and food distribution airlift.
2. Emergency Fuel & Food Relief (2022 Sri Lanka Financial Crisis): Delivery of credit lines, essential grain, and diesel supplies.

section_d.title: Section D: Competency / Source-Based Case Study (6 Marks)
section_d.instructions: Read the passage carefully and answer the sub-questions that follow.
section_d.case_scenario: Passage: In March 2023, a tropical cyclone caused catastrophic flooding across a low-lying Indian Ocean island nation, contaminating coastal drinking wells and disrupting electricity grids. Within 12 hours of receiving an emergency request, the Indian Navy dispatched two stealth frigates carrying 20 tons of relief material. Indian naval engineers installed solar-powered water filtration units generating 10,000 liters of pure water daily. Indian medical corps established emergency clinics treating over 1,500 flood victims, while joint naval patrols secured sea lanes against maritime piracy.

sub_questions.question_text: Which foreign policy vision guided India's swift naval response in this scenario? (2 Marks)
sub_questions.solution_and_marking_scheme: India's 'Neighborhood First' policy and SAGAR ('Security and Growth for All in the Region') vision, which commits India to maritime security and HADR first-responder assistance in the Indian Ocean (2 Marks).

sub_questions.question_text: Identify two distinct types of humanitarian relief provided by the naval mission. (2 Marks)
sub_questions.solution_and_marking_scheme:
1. Medical Relief: Setting up emergency clinics to treat over 1,500 flood victims (1 Mark).
2. Engineering & Public Health Relief: Deploying solar-powered water filtration units to restore safe drinking water (1 Mark).

sub_questions.question_text: Why are joint maritime surveillance patrols vital for both India and island neighbours? (2 Marks)
sub_questions.solution_and_marking_scheme: Joint surveillance secures vital Indian Ocean sea lanes against non-traditional security threats like piracy, illegal fishing, and smuggling, preserving oceanic trade stability for all littoral nations (2 Marks).

model_paper.paper_title: Chapter 3 Model Assessment - Empires and Kingdoms: 6th to 10th Centuries

section_a.title: Section A: Objective MCQs & Assertion-Reason (6 Marks)
section_a.instructions: Answer all questions. Each question carries 1 mark.

questions.question_text: Which Chalukya ruler defeated Emperor Harshavardhana on the banks of the Narmada River?

Which three dynasties were involved in the centuries-long Tripartite Struggle for control over Kannauj?

Assertion (A): Control over Kannauj became the prime objective of northern and deccan powers from the 8th to 10th centuries.
Reason (R): Kannauj symbolized imperial sovereignty after Harsha and commanded the lucrative Gangetic trade routes.
options: A) Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.

D) A is false but R is true.
questions.correct_option: A) Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
questions.marking_scheme: 1 Mark for establishing economic and political motives behind the Tripartite Struggle.

questions.question_text:
Assertion (A): The Kudavolai system described in Uttaramerur inscriptions represented an advanced local democratic process.
Reason (R): Village committee members were chosen by drawing palm-leaf tickets from an earthen pot after verifying eligibility qualifications.
options: A) Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
B) Both A and R are true, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
C) A is true but R is false.
D) A is false but R is true.

section_b.title: Section B: Short Answer Questions (10 Marks)
section_b.instructions: Answer all 5 questions. Each question carries 2 marks.

questions.question_text: Name the capital city of Harshavardhana and list two literary sources that document his reign.
questions.solution_and_marking_scheme:
Capital: Kannauj (1 Mark).
Literary Sources: Harshacharita by Banabhatta, and Travelogue (Si-Yu-Ki) by Chinese pilgrim Xuanzang (1 Mark).

questions.question_text: Differentiate between the Sabha and the Ur in South Indian village administration.
questions.solution_and_marking_scheme:
Sabha: Autonomous assembly of Brahmin landholders in Brahmadeya villages (1 Mark).
Ur: General village assembly open to landholders in non-Brahmin agrarian settlements (1 Mark).

questions.question_text: Explain the role of Samantas in the early medieval feudal political structure.
questions.solution_and_marking_scheme: Samantas were subordinate regional chieftains or landholders who provided military contingents during wars, paid annual tribute to the king, and attended imperial assemblies. When central power weakened, Samantas often declared independence (2 Marks).

questions.question_text: Which Pala king founded Vikramashila University and what was its major academic focus?
questions.solution_and_marking_scheme: King Dharmapala of the Pala Dynasty founded Vikramashila University (1 Mark). Its primary academic focus was Mahayana and Vajrayana Buddhist philosophy, logic, and Sanskrit grammar (1 Mark).

questions.question_text: Identify the key architectural contributions of the Pallavas at Mamallapuram.
questions.solution_and_marking_scheme: The Pallavas constructed monolithic rock-cut cave temples, the monolithic Pancha Rathas (Five Chariots), and the structural Shore Temple overlooking the Bay of Bengal (2 Marks).

section_c.title: Section C: Long Answer & Analytical Questions (8 Marks)
section_c.instructions: Answer both questions. Each question carries 4 marks.

questions.question_text: Analyze the Kudavolai system of election recorded in the Uttaramerur inscriptions. Detail the candidate qualifications, sub-committees, and voting mechanism.
questions.solution_and_marking_scheme:
1. Candidate Qualifications: Ownership of taxable land, age between 35 and 70, knowledge of Vedic texts, moral integrity, and clean financial record (1 Mark).
2. Sub-Committees (Variyams): Special committees for tank irrigation, gardens, gold, taxation, and justice (1 Mark).
3. Voting Mechanism: Names of qualified candidates were written on palm-leaf tickets (kudavolai) and placed in an earthen pot (1 Mark).
4. Selection: In a full village assembly, a young boy drew tickets out of the pot to select committee members impartially (1 Mark).

questions.question_text: Describe the architectural marvel of the Kailashanatha Temple at Ellora (Cave 16) and explain why it represents an unprecedented engineering achievement.
questions.solution_and_marking_scheme:
1. Monolithic Excavation: Carved top-down from a single volcanic basalt mountain cliff under Rashtrakuta King Krishna I (1 Mark).
2. Scale & Scale Removal: Workers excavated over 200,000 tons of solid rock without modern machinery or scaffolding (1 Mark).
3. Architectural Components: Features a multi-storeyed vimana, gateway (gopuram), courtyard, free-standing pillars, and life-sized elephant sculptures (1 Mark).
4. Artistic Mastery: Intricate relief panels depicting scenes from Ramayana, Mahabharata, and Shiva's cosmic dance (1 Mark).

section_d.title: Section D: Competency / Source-Based Case Study (6 Marks)
section_d.instructions: Read the passage carefully and answer the sub-questions that follow.
section_d.case_scenario: Passage: In the 8th century, King Krishna I issued a copper-plate charter granting a tax-free village near the Narmada River to 30 scholars. The charter, engraved in Sanskrit with the royal Rashtrakuta seal, specified that the scholars had the right to cultivate forest plots, construct irrigation tanks, and collect local market taxes. In return, the scholars established a Vedic math school (ghatika) and maintained a public manuscript repository. Local Samantas were instructed by royal decree not to interfere with the village's internal administration.

sub_questions.question_text: What type of land grant is described in this copper-plate charter? (2 Marks)
sub_questions.solution_and_marking_scheme: A Brahmadeya land grant (tax-free grant gifted to learned scholars/Brahmins) issued directly by the king (2 Marks).

sub_questions.question_text: Identify two socio-economic benefits the kingdom derived from issuing such charters. (2 Marks)
sub_questions.solution_and_marking_scheme:
1. Agrarian Expansion: Bringing uncultivated forest lands under systematic farming and irrigation (1 Mark).
2. Educational & Administrative Spread: Promoting Sanskrit scholarship, literacy, and establishing royal influence in rural areas (1 Mark).

sub_questions.question_text: Why did the king explicitly instruct Samantas not to interfere in the granted village? (2 Marks)
sub_questions.solution_and_marking_scheme: To guarantee the administrative autonomy and tax-exempt status of the Brahmadeya village, preventing local feudatories from levying unauthorized taxes or usurping royal authority (2 Marks).

model_paper.paper_title: Chapter 4 Model Assessment - Turning Tides: 11th and 12th Centuries

section_a.title: Section A: Objective MCQs & Assertion-Reason (6 Marks)
section_a.instructions: Answer all questions. Each question carries 1 mark.

questions.question_text: In which battle did Muhammad Ghuri defeat Prithviraj Chauhan, laying the political foundation for Turkic rule in Delhi?
options: A) First Battle of Tarain (1191 CE)
B) Second Battle of Tarain (1192 CE)

questions.question_text: Who was the author of the scientific Arabic text 'Kitab al-Hind'?
Which Chola emperor executed an overseas naval campaign across the Bay of Bengal against the Srivijaya Empire in 1025 CE?
Which 12th-century Sanskrit mathematical treatise was composed in poetic verse by Bhaskaracharya II?

Assertion (A): The military campaigns of Mahmud of Ghazni differed fundamentally from those of Muhammad Ghuri.
Reason (R): Mahmud of Ghazni focused on plundering temple wealth without permanent annexation, whereas Ghuri aimed at territorial conquest.
options: A) Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
B) Both A and R are true, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
C) A is true but R is false.
D) A is false but R is true.
questions.correct_option: A) Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
questions.marking_scheme: 1 Mark for establishing the strategic distinction between Ghaznavid plunder and Ghurid annexation.

questions.question_text:
Assertion (A): The Chola naval campaign against Srivijaya secured Indian maritime trade routes to China.
Reason (R): Autonomous merchant guilds like Ayyavole financed Chola naval fleets to eliminate pirate blockades in the Malacca Strait.
options: A) Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
B) Both A and R are true, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
C) A is true but R is false.
D) A is false but R is true.

section_b.title: Section B: Short Answer Questions (10 Marks)
section_b.instructions: Answer all 5 questions. Each question carries 2 marks.

questions.question_text: Contrast the outcomes of the First and Second Battles of Tarain (1191 and 1192 CE).
questions.solution_and_marking_scheme:
First Battle (1191 CE): Prithviraj Chauhan defeated Muhammad Ghuri (1 Mark).
Second Battle (1192 CE): Muhammad Ghuri defeated Prithviraj Chauhan, establishing Turkic military supremacy in northern India (1 Mark).

questions.question_text: How did Al-Biruni gather information for writing 'Kitab al-Hind'?
questions.solution_and_marking_scheme: Al-Biruni learned Sanskrit, resided in India for several years, collaborated directly with Hindu pandits, and studied original Sanskrit texts on philosophy, astronomy, and law (2 Marks).

questions.question_text: State the historical significance of Chola naval expansion under Rajendra I.
questions.solution_and_marking_scheme: Rajendra I built a formidable blue-water navy that crossed the Bay of Bengal, conquered ports in Sumatra/Malacca (Srivijaya), secured international sea trade corridors to Song China, and established Chola maritime hegemony (2 Marks).

questions.question_text: Name two major merchant guilds active during the Chola period and describe their function.
questions.solution_and_marking_scheme:
Guilds: Ayyavole (Five Hundred Swamis) and Manigramam (1 Mark).
Function: They organized long-distance overland and maritime trade, operated armed security escorts, issued commercial credit, and built temple complexes (1 Mark).

questions.question_text: Identify the key architectural features of the Konark Sun Temple built by the Eastern Ganga Dynasty.
questions.solution_and_marking_scheme: Designed as a giant stone chariot for Sun God Surya, featuring 24 intricately carved stone wheels (functioning as sun-dials) pulled by 7 rearing horses in Kalinga architectural style (2 Marks).

section_c.title: Section C: Long Answer & Analytical Questions (8 Marks)
section_c.instructions: Answer both questions. Each question carries 4 marks.

questions.question_text: Why are the 11th and 12th centuries designated as a period of 'Turning Tides' in Indian history? Evaluate both northern political shifts and southern achievements.
questions.solution_and_marking_scheme:
Northern Political Shifts (2 Marks):
- Incursions of Ghaznavids and Ghurid conquests dismantled traditional Rajput kingdoms.
- Defeat of Prithviraj Chauhan at Tarain (1192 CE) led to the establishment of the Delhi Sultanate, altering northern political structures.
Southern & Cultural Heights (2 Marks):
- Peninsular India reached peak maritime power through Chola naval expeditions across Southeast Asia.
- Zenith of monumental temple architecture (Brihadishvara at Thanjavur, Kandariya Mahadeva at Khajuraho) and mathematical breakthroughs like Bhaskara's Lilavati.

questions.question_text: Discuss the impact of the destruction of monastic universities like Nalanda on Indian education, and explain how scientific knowledge nevertheless survived.
questions.solution_and_marking_scheme:
Impact of Destruction (2 Marks):
- Burning of university manuscript archives (Dharmaganja) destroyed thousands of original scientific, philosophical, and medical texts.
- Dispersal of monastic scholars disrupted centralized commentary and teaching networks.
Mechanisms of Survival (2 Marks):
- Scientific traditions were decentralized across regional royal courts (Paramaras, Cholas), temple math schools, and family scholar lineages (like Bhaskaracharya II).
- Scholars carried copies of palm-leaf manuscripts to Nepal, Tibet, and South India, preserving knowledge through oral and written transmission.

section_d.title: Section D: Competency / Source-Based Case Study (6 Marks)
section_d.instructions: Read the passage carefully and answer the sub-questions that follow.
section_d.case_scenario: Passage: In his 1030 CE text 'Kitab al-Hind', the Persian scholar Al-Biruni wrote: 'The Hindus believe that there is no country like theirs, no nation like theirs, no king like theirs, no religion like theirs, no science like theirs. They are haughty, foolishly vain, self-sufficient, and stolid. If they traveled and mixed with other nations, they would soon change their mind.' Al-Biruni spent over a decade studying Sanskrit texts on mathematics, astronomy, and philosophy alongside Indian pandits, noting both their brilliant decimal numeral system and their rigid social stratification.

sub_questions.question_text: What criticism did Al-Biruni level against 11th-century Indian scholars in this passage? (2 Marks)
sub_questions.solution_and_marking_scheme: Al-Biruni criticized Indian scholars for intellectual isolation, excessive self-sufficiency, and reluctance to travel or learn from foreign societies (2 Marks).

sub_questions.question_text: Which specific Indian scientific achievements did Al-Biruni praise despite his criticisms? (2 Marks)
sub_questions.solution_and_marking_scheme: He praised the Indian decimal numeral system, place-value notation, zero, advanced astronomical calculations, and mathematical treatises (2 Marks).

sub_questions.question_text: Why is 'Kitab al-Hind' considered an invaluable primary source for historians studying 11th-century India? (2 Marks)
sub_questions.solution_and_marking_scheme: Because Al-Biruni provided an objective, highly detailed Arabic scientific record based on direct Sanskrit textual study, covering law, religion, caste social structure, mathematics, and geography without blind bias (2 Marks).

model_paper.paper_title: Chapter 5 Model Assessment - India, a Home to Many

section_b.title: Section B: Short Answer Questions (10 Marks)
section_b.instructions: Answer all 5 questions. Each question carries 2 marks.

questions.question_text: Translate and explain the philosophical meaning of 'Vasudhaiva Kutumbakam'.
questions.solution_and_marking_scheme: Translates to 'The whole world is one family' from the Maha Upanishad (1 Mark). It expresses a universal worldview of kinship, tolerance, and sanctuary for all human beings (1 Mark).

questions.question_text: Narrate the legend of 'Milk and Sugar' associated with the Parsi arrival at Sanjan.
questions.solution_and_marking_scheme: King Jadi Rana presented a bowl filled with milk to show his kingdom was full. The Parsi priest stirred sugar into the milk without spilling a drop, symbolizing that Parsis would sweeten and enrich society without overflowing or causing conflict (2 Marks).

questions.question_text: Name two distinct Jewish communities that settled along India's western coast.
questions.solution_and_marking_scheme:
1. Cochin Jews along the Malabar Coast of Kerala (1 Mark).
2. Bene Israel along the Konkan Coast of Maharashtra (1 Mark).

questions.question_text: How do the Siddis preserve their African cultural heritage in modern India?
questions.solution_and_marking_scheme: They preserve the 'Siddi Dhamal' folk performance, combining East African percussion rhythms, drum beats, and spiritual songs with regional Gujarati/Kannada lyrics (2 Marks).

questions.question_text: State the achievements of Siddi community leader Hirabai Lobi.
questions.solution_and_marking_scheme: Hirabai Lobi founded self-help financial groups, organic farming units, and women's literacy centers in Gujarat, for which she was awarded the Padma Shri in 2023 (2 Marks).

section_c.title: Section C: Long Answer & Analytical Questions (8 Marks)
section_c.instructions: Answer both questions. Each question carries 4 marks.

questions.question_text: Differentiate between forced cultural assimilation and Indian pluralism using historical case studies of sanctuary communities (Parsis, Cochin Jews, Syriac Christians).
questions.solution_and_marking_scheme:
Forced Assimilation Concept (1 Mark):
- Requires incoming migrant groups to abandon their original faith, language, and culture to merge completely into the dominant culture.
Indian Pluralism Framework (1 Mark):
- Granted religious freedom, land grants, and legal autonomy, allowing refugees to retain their faith while adopting local languages and attire.
Historical Examples (2 Marks):
1. Parsis preserved Zoroastrian fire temples while adopting Gujarati language and attire.
2. Cochin Jews built synagogues in Kerala style and spoke Malayalam while maintaining Hebrew liturgy.
3. Syriac Christians integrated into Kerala society while retaining Syriac liturgical traditions.

questions.question_text: Examine how the ethos of 'Vasudhaiva Kutumbakam' operates bidirectionally in modern times, particularly regarding the global Indian diaspora.
questions.solution_and_marking_scheme:
Inward Dimension (2 Marks):
- Historically, India welcomed persecuted global communities (Parsis, Jews, Tibetans) providing sanctuary and equal citizenship.
Outward Dimension (2 Marks):
- The modern Indian diaspora living in host nations across the Americas, Europe, Middle East, and Asia carries these values.
- Indian emigrants integrate peacefully, contribute as law-abiding citizens, entrepreneurs, scientists, and civic leaders, fostering global intercultural harmony.

section_d.title: Section D: Competency / Source-Based Case Study (6 Marks)
section_d.instructions: Read the passage carefully and answer the sub-questions that follow.
section_d.case_scenario: Passage: The Paradesi Synagogue in Mattancherry, Cochin, constructed in 1568 CE under the patronage of the Raja of Cochin, stands next to the Mattancherry Palace temple. The synagogue features a tiled roof reflecting Kerala traditional architecture, hand-painted blue-and-white willow pattern porcelain tiles imported from Canton, China (1762), and crystal chandeliers from Belgium. The Cochin Jewish community spoke fluent Malayalam, wore traditional Kerala garments, and contributed actively to spice trade and public administration while celebrating Sabbath in Hebrew.

sub_questions.question_text: Identify two distinct architectural/artistic influences present in the Paradesi Synagogue. (2 Marks)
sub_questions.solution_and_marking_scheme:
1. Traditional Kerala architecture (tiled roofs and local woodwork) (1 Mark).
2. Chinese craftsmanship (hand-painted blue willow porcelain floor tiles) and Belgian glass chandeliers (1 Mark).

sub_questions.question_text: How does the proximity of the synagogue to the Raja's palace temple reflect Indian sanctuary traditions? (2 Marks)
sub_questions.solution_and_marking_scheme: Placing a Jewish place of worship directly adjacent to the royal Hindu palace temple proves royal patronage, religious tolerance, and mutual respect without communal segregation (2 Marks).

sub_questions.question_text: Explain how the Cochin Jewish community demonstrated cultural synthesis without losing religious identity. (2 Marks)
sub_questions.solution_and_marking_scheme: They adopted local Malayalam language, attire, and trading practices while maintaining Hebrew religious liturgy, kosher dietary laws, and Sabbath observances (2 Marks).

chapters.chapter_title: The State, the Government, and You

model_paper.paper_title: Chapter 6 Model Assessment - The State, the Government, and You

section_a.title: Section A: Objective MCQs & Assertion-Reason (6 Marks)
section_a.instructions: Answer all questions. Each question carries 1 mark.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is NOT one of the four essential elements of a State?
Why is India defined as a 'Republic' in the Preamble to its Constitution?
options: A) Its Head of State (President) is an elected citizen holding office for a fixed term.
B) It has a bicameral Parliament.
C) It conducts elections every five years.
D) Its Prime Minister is the head of government.
questions.correct_option: A) Its Head of State (President) is an elected citizen holding office for a fixed term.

questions.question_text: Which organ of government is primarily responsible for enacting and amending public laws?
What constitutional mechanism empowers the Supreme Court to strike down unconstitutional laws?

Assertion (A): The State is a permanent political organization, whereas the Government changes periodically.
Reason (R): The Government is the elected agency that executes state power for a fixed tenure, while the State represents the enduring sovereign nation.
options: A) Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
B) Both A and R are true, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
C) A is true but R is false.
D) A is false but R is true.
questions.correct_option: A) Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
questions.marking_scheme: 1 Mark for distinguishing the permanent State from the temporary Government.

questions.question_text:
Assertion (A): Separation of powers among Legislature, Executive, and Judiciary prevents tyranny.
Reason (R): Checks and balances ensure no single organ accumulates unchecked supreme power.
options: A) Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
B) Both A and R are true, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
C) A is true but R is false.
D) A is false but R is true.
questions.correct_option: A) Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
questions.marking_scheme: 1 Mark for linking separation of powers with the prevention of authoritarian rule.

section_b.title: Section B: Short Answer Questions (10 Marks)
section_b.instructions: Answer all 5 questions. Each question carries 2 marks.

questions.question_text: List the four essential elements required to form a State.
questions.solution_and_marking_scheme:
1. Defined Territory
2. Permanent Population
3. Functioning Government
4. Sovereignty (2 Marks for all 4 named accurately).

questions.question_text: Distinguish between a State and a Government.
questions.solution_and_marking_scheme:
State: Permanent, abstract political entity comprising territory, population, government, and sovereignty (1 Mark).
Government: Temporary administrative body of elected/appointed officials managing state affairs for a fixed tenure (1 Mark).

questions.question_text: Explain why Sovereignty is the defining legal element of a State.
questions.solution_and_marking_scheme: Sovereignty gives a state supreme, independent legal authority to make internal laws and conduct foreign policy without external dictation or colonial control (2 Marks).

questions.question_text: State the primary functions of the three organs of government.
questions.solution_and_marking_scheme:
1. Legislature: Enacts and frames laws.
2. Executive: Enforces and implements laws.
3. Judiciary: Interprets laws and administers justice (2 Marks).

questions.question_text: How do citizens participate actively in a democracy beyond casting votes during elections?
questions.solution_and_marking_scheme: By questioning public policies, filing Right to Information (RTI) applications, participating in peaceful civic assemblies, and holding elected representatives accountable (2 Marks).

section_c.title: Section C: Long Answer & Analytical Questions (8 Marks)
section_c.instructions: Answer both questions. Each question carries 4 marks.

questions.question_text: Analyze the system of Separation of Powers and Checks & Balances among the Legislature, Executive, and Judiciary in India.
questions.solution_and_marking_scheme:
Separation of Powers Concept (1 Mark):
- Power is divided among three independent organs so no single organ holds absolute control.
Checks & Balances Mechanisms (3 Marks):
1. Executive - Legislature Check: The Prime Minister and Cabinet are drawn from Parliament and must maintain the confidence of the Lok Sabha.
2. Judiciary - Legislature Check: The Supreme Court can exercise Judicial Review to strike down unconstitutional parliamentary laws.
3. Executive - Judiciary Check: Judges are appointed by the Executive, but can only be removed through a stringent impeachment process by Parliament.

questions.question_text: Explain why India is designated as both a 'Democratic' and a 'Republic' state. Contrast a Republic with a Hereditary Monarchy.
questions.solution_and_marking_scheme:
Democratic Feature (1 Mark):
- Supreme power resides in the people, who exercise sovereignty through universal adult franchise and competitive elections.
Republic Feature (1 Mark):
- The Head of State (President of India) is an elected citizen holding office for a fixed 5-year term.
Contrast with Monarchy (2 Marks):
- In a Hereditary Monarchy (e.g., UK), the Head of State inherits the position by royal bloodline rather than election.
- In a Republic, any eligible citizen, regardless of birth, can potentially be elected Head of State.

section_d.title: Section D: Competency / Source-Based Case Study (6 Marks)
section_d.instructions: Read the passage carefully and answer the sub-questions that follow.
section_d.case_scenario: Passage: In a municipal town, the state assembly passed a regional law banning citizens from assembling in public parks to voice grievances regarding water shortages. A civic group filed a petition before the High Court arguing that the law violated their fundamental right to peaceful assembly guaranteed under Article 19. The High Court issued a stay order, examined the assembly statute, and struck down the municipal restriction as unconstitutional, ordering the police to allow peaceful civic meetings.

sub_questions.question_text: Which organ of government enacted the contested law, and which organ struck it down? (2 Marks)
sub_questions.solution_and_marking_scheme:
Enacted by: The Legislature (State Assembly) (1 Mark).
Struck down by: The Judiciary (High Court) (1 Mark).

sub_questions.question_text: What constitutional power did the High Court exercise to invalidate the assembly law? (2 Marks)
sub_questions.solution_and_marking_scheme: Judicial Review—the constitutional power of High Courts and the Supreme Court to declare any legislative act void if it violates Fundamental Rights or constitutional principles (2 Marks).

sub_questions.question_text: How does this scenario illustrate the protection of citizen rights against legislative overreach? (2 Marks)
sub_questions.solution_and_marking_scheme: It proves that in a constitutional democracy, temporary elected majorities in the Legislature cannot override Fundamental Rights. An independent Judiciary acts as the guardian of the Constitution to protect citizens (2 Marks).

model_paper.paper_title: Chapter 7 Model Assessment - Infrastructure: Engine of India's Development

section_a.title: Section A: Objective MCQs & Assertion-Reason (6 Marks)
section_a.instructions: Answer all questions. Each question carries 1 mark.

questions.question_text: Which bridge connecting Mumbai with Navi Mumbai is India's longest sea bridge (~21.8 km)?
What bio-engineered living structures are crafted by Khasi tribes in Meghalaya using rubber fig tree roots?
Cochin International Airport in Kerala set a global benchmark in 2015 by becoming the world's first airport to run entirely on:
Which central government scheme is dedicated to constructing all-weather paved roads connecting rural Indian villages?
options: A) PMGSY (Pradhan Mantri Gram Sadak Yojana)
questions.correct_option: A) PMGSY (Pradhan Mantri Gram Sadak Yojana)

questions.question_text:
Assertion (A): Physical infrastructure acts as a force multiplier for national economic growth.
Reason (R): Modern transport, energy, water, and digital networks lower logistics freight costs and enable market access.
options: A) Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
B) Both A and R are true, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
C) A is true but R is false.
D) A is false but R is true.
questions.correct_option: A) Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
questions.marking_scheme: 1 Mark for establishing the economic multiplier mechanism.

questions.question_text:
Assertion (A): Jingkieng Jri (Living Root Bridges) grow stronger over time unlike concrete bridges.
Reason (R): Concrete degrades under humidity, whereas living roots of Ficus elastica continue growing thicker and self-healing over decades.
options: A) Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
B) Both A and R are true, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
C) A is true but R is false.
D) A is false but R is true.
questions.correct_option: A) Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
questions.marking_scheme: 1 Mark for linking root biological growth with structural longevity.

section_b.title: Section B: Short Answer Questions (10 Marks)
section_b.instructions: Answer all 5 questions. Each question carries 2 marks.

questions.question_text: List the four primary pillars of physical infrastructure with one example each.
questions.solution_and_marking_scheme:
1. Transport (Expressways, Atal Setu)
2. Energy (Solar parks, Power Grid)
3. Water & Sanitation (Canal networks, dams)
4. Digital Communication (Fiber optics, 5G towers) (2 Marks for all 4 listed).

questions.question_text: Explain why physical infrastructure is called a 'Force Multiplier' for development.
questions.solution_and_marking_scheme: Because upgrading infrastructure simultaneously lowers transportation costs, prevents agricultural post-harvest spoilage, powers factories, connects rural populations to hospitals/schools, and attracts investment (2 Marks).

questions.question_text: Describe the bio-engineering process behind Jingkieng Jri (Living Root Bridges) in Meghalaya.
questions.solution_and_marking_scheme: Khasi tribes guide aerial roots of living rubber fig trees (Ficus elastica) across mountain streams using hollowed betel nut trunks over 15 to 30 years. The roots intertwine, root into opposite banks, and grow thicker over decades (2 Marks).

questions.question_text: State the significance of the Chenab Rail Bridge in Jammu & Kashmir.
questions.solution_and_marking_scheme: It is the world's highest railway arch bridge (~359 meters above the riverbed), connecting the Kashmir Valley with the national Indian Railway network in all weather conditions (2 Marks).

questions.question_text: Why is civic responsibility crucial for the maintenance of public infrastructure?
questions.solution_and_marking_scheme: Public infrastructure is constructed using taxpayer money. Vandalism, littering, stealing fittings, or damaging transport property drains public funds into avoidable repairs rather than new development (2 Marks).

section_c.title: Section C: Long Answer & Analytical Questions (8 Marks)
section_c.instructions: Answer both questions. Each question carries 4 marks.

questions.question_text: Compare traditional concrete bridge engineering with indigenous living root bridge (Jingkieng Jri) architecture across materials, construction timeline, lifespan, and environmental impact.
questions.solution_and_marking_scheme:
1. Materials: Concrete bridges use steel, cement, and crushed stone; Root bridges use living roots of Ficus elastica trees (1 Mark).
2. Timeline & Labor: Concrete bridges build quickly (2-4 years); Root bridges take 15-30 years of patient guidance (1 Mark).
3. Lifespan: Concrete degrades over 50-100 years due to rust and weathering; Root bridges last 500+ years and grow stronger with age (1 Mark).
4. Environmental Impact: Concrete manufacturing emits high carbon; Root bridges have zero carbon footprint, absorb rainfall, and preserve forest ecosystems (1 Mark).

questions.question_text: Examine the role of green infrastructure in combating climate change, highlighting Cochin International Airport and Muppandal Wind Farm.
questions.solution_and_marking_scheme:
Green Infrastructure Concept (1 Mark):
- Shifting infrastructure energy supplies from fossil fuels to zero-emission renewable sources.
Cochin Airport Example (1.5 Marks):
- Installed a 46,000 solar panel facility in 2015, becoming the world's first 100% solar-powered airport, eliminating over 300,000 tons of carbon emissions.
Muppandal Wind Farm Example (1.5 Marks):
- Onshore wind farm in Tamil Nadu leveraging monsoon winds to generate clean electricity for millions of homes and industries.

section_d.title: Section D: Competency / Source-Based Case Study (6 Marks)
section_d.instructions: Read the passage carefully and answer the sub-questions that follow.
section_d.case_scenario: Passage: Before 2018, farmers in a mountain district in Himachal Pradesh lost 35% of their apple harvest due to unpaved roads that became muddy during monsoon rains. Truck drivers charged high freight rates, and apples reached Delhi markets bruised. Under a rural connectivity initiative, the government constructed an all-weather double-lane road with a 2-kilometer mountain tunnel and installed a solar-powered cold storage hub near the highway. Freight charges dropped by 30%, transport time was cut from 14 hours to 5 hours, and farmers' annual incomes rose by 45%.

sub_questions.question_text: Identify two types of physical infrastructure constructed in this mountain district. (2 Marks)
sub_questions.solution_and_marking_scheme:
1. Transport Infrastructure: All-weather double-lane highway with a mountain tunnel (1 Mark).
2. Energy & Logistics Infrastructure: Solar-powered cold storage facility (1 Mark).

sub_questions.question_text: How did the new highway and cold storage facility impact apple farmers' income? (2 Marks)
sub_questions.solution_and_marking_scheme: By cutting transport time from 14 to 5 hours and preventing spoilage through cold storage, apples reached markets fresh without damage, allowing farmers to command higher prices and increase incomes by 45% (2 Marks).

sub_questions.question_text: Explain how this scenario illustrates infrastructure as an economic force multiplier bridging rural-urban divides. (2 Marks)
sub_questions.solution_and_marking_scheme: It shows that transport and energy links directly connect isolated mountain farmers to lucrative urban consumer markets in Delhi, lowering freight costs and driving rural economic growth (2 Marks).

chapters.chapter_title: Banks and the Magic of Finance

model_paper.paper_title: Chapter 8 Model Assessment - Banks and the Magic of Finance

section_a.title: Section A: Objective MCQs & Assertion-Reason (6 Marks)
section_a.instructions: Answer all questions. Each question carries 1 mark.

questions.question_text: What is the apex regulatory bank responsible for supervising commercial banks and issuing currency in India?
Which mobile digital payment system developed by NPCI allows instant real-time bank transactions via QR codes?
The difference between the higher interest rate charged on loans and the lower interest rate paid on customer deposits is called:
Which type of bank account pays zero interest and is designed specifically for traders and business owners needing unlimited daily transactions?

Assertion (A): Compound interest yields significantly higher returns over time compared to simple interest.
Reason (R): Compound interest calculates interest on both the initial principal and the accumulated interest from prior periods.
options: A) Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
B) Both A and R are true, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
C) A is true but R is false.
D) A is false but R is true.
questions.correct_option: A) Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
questions.marking_scheme: 1 Mark for connecting compounding logic with exponential financial growth.

questions.question_text:
Assertion (A): Formal bank credit is far safer for rural farmers than informal moneylender loans.
Reason (R): Commercial banks operate under strict RBI regulation with legal interest caps, whereas informal moneylenders charge exorbitant interest leading to debt traps.
options: A) Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
B) Both A and R are true, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
C) A is true but R is false.
D) A is false but R is true.
questions.correct_option: A) Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
questions.marking_scheme: 1 Mark for establishing regulatory protection offered by formal banks.

section_b.title: Section B: Short Answer Questions (10 Marks)
section_b.instructions: Answer all 5 questions. Each question carries 2 marks.

questions.question_text: Explain the concept of financial intermediation in commercial banking.
questions.solution_and_marking_scheme: Banks act as intermediaries collecting surplus funds from depositors (savers) and pooling them to extend credit/loans to borrowers (entrepreneurs, farmers, home buyers) (2 Marks).

questions.question_text: Define Interest Spread and state how it generates income for commercial banks.
questions.solution_and_marking_scheme: Interest Spread is the difference between the higher interest rate charged on loans (~9-12%) and the lower interest rate paid on deposits (~3-4%). This margin covers operational costs and forms bank profit (2 Marks).

questions.question_text: Differentiate between a Savings Account and a Current Account.
questions.solution_and_marking_scheme:
Savings Account: For individuals to save money; pays modest interest; has daily withdrawal limits (1 Mark).
Current Account: For business owners; pays zero interest; allows unlimited daily transactions and overdraft facility (1 Mark).

questions.question_text: State two key regulatory roles of the Reserve Bank of India (RBI).
questions.solution_and_marking_scheme:
1. Supervising commercial bank operations and setting interest guidelines (1 Mark).
2. Managing monetary policy, controlling inflation, and issuing national currency notes (1 Mark).

questions.question_text: How has UPI transformed small street-vendor businesses in India?
questions.solution_and_marking_scheme: UPI enables instant cashless payments directly into bank accounts via smartphone QR codes, eliminating cash handling risks, exact change issues, and providing formal digital transaction records for credit access (2 Marks).

section_c.title: Section C: Long Answer & Analytical Questions (8 Marks)
section_c.instructions: Answer both questions. Each question carries 4 marks.

questions.question_text: Calculate and compare the returns on a principal deposit of ₹10,000 over 3 years at an annual interest rate of 10% under Simple Interest (SI) versus Compound Interest (CI). Explain why CI produces a higher return.
questions.solution_and_marking_scheme:
Simple Interest Calculation (1.5 Marks):
- SI = (P × R × T) / 100 = (10,000 × 10 × 3) / 100 = ₹3,000.
- Total Amount = ₹10,000 + ₹3,000 = ₹13,000.
Compound Interest Calculation (1.5 Marks):
- Year 1 Interest: 10% of ₹10,000 = ₹1,000 (New Principal = ₹11,000).
- Year 2 Interest: 10% of ₹11,000 = ₹1,100 (New Principal = ₹12,100).
- Year 3 Interest: 10% of ₹12,100 = ₹1,210.
- Total Interest = ₹1,000 + ₹1,100 + ₹1,210 = ₹3,310. Total Amount = ₹13,310.
Reasoning (1 Mark):
- CI yields ₹310 more because interest in Years 2 and 3 is calculated on the growing accumulated balance (interest earned on interest), whereas SI calculates interest strictly on the initial ₹10,000 principal.

questions.question_text: Relate the ancient Chessboard Wheat Grain Legend to the financial power of compounding. What lesson does it teach investors and borrowers?
questions.solution_and_marking_scheme:
Chessboard Legend Summary (2 Marks):
- The inventor asked the King for 1 grain of wheat on square 1, doubling on each subsequent square (2, 4, 8, 16...).
- By square 64, the required grains equaled 2^64 - 1 = 18.44 quintillion grains, exceeding world wheat production, proving geometric doubling power.
Financial Lesson for Investors & Borrowers (2 Marks):
- For Savers: Compounding builds exponential wealth over time if savings are invested early and left to grow.
- For Borrowers: High-interest debts (especially from informal moneylenders) compound rapidly if unpaid, leading to catastrophic debt traps.

section_d.title: Section D: Competency / Source-Based Case Study (6 Marks)
section_d.instructions: Read the passage carefully and answer the sub-questions that follow.
section_d.case_scenario: Passage: Sunita, a pottery artisan in Odisha, needed ₹40,000 to buy an electric potter's wheel and kiln. A local moneylender offered cash instantly at 3% interest per month (36% simple interest per year) without requiring documents. A local commercial bank offered an artisan loan at 9% per year but required her to complete Know Your Customer (KYC) identity documentation (Aadhaar and PAN card) and open a savings account. Sunita chose the bank, submitted her KYC, and received the loan. After buying the kiln, her pottery production doubled, and she repaid the loan in monthly installments via UPI.

sub_questions.question_text: Compare the annual interest cost Sunita would pay under the moneylender vs the commercial bank. (2 Marks)
sub_questions.solution_and_marking_scheme:
Moneylender Cost: 36% of ₹40,000 = ₹14,400 interest per year (1 Mark).
Bank Cost: 9% of ₹40,000 = ₹3,600 interest per year. Sunita saved ₹10,800 annually by choosing the bank (1 Mark).

sub_questions.question_text: Why was fulfilling the bank's KYC documentation a crucial step for Sunita's financial inclusion? (2 Marks)
sub_questions.solution_and_marking_scheme: KYC documentation verified her identity, opening formal banking access, establishing her credit history, and protecting her from unregulated moneylender exploitation (2 Marks).

sub_questions.question_text: How did combining formal bank credit with UPI payments empower Sunita's business growth? (2 Marks)
sub_questions.solution_and_marking_scheme: Formal bank credit provided low-cost capital to double production, while UPI enabled seamless monthly loan repayments and instant digital payments from urban pottery buyers (2 Marks).
